c024_1789-03-25.summary: Postscript to the duplicate: Deboli will ask in every letter what Hetman Branicki is doing; the Prince of Nassau-Siegen writes that Branicki is one of the most devoted to Russia; Russia wants no new war.
c024_1789-03-25.en:
Postscript. Having already written the letter, the following thought comes to me: that I shall make it a habit, often in
my letters, to [repeat?] this question: what is Hetman Branicki doing. The plans of others [?] I do understand, as
from [...], but not his. With all that, in which I beg Your Majesty for secrecy: the Prince of Nassau writes here that
Branicki is one of the most attached to Russia. Good God! This Prince of Nassau, who [...] receiving Your Majesty's
[letter], had no time for Your Majesty's answer at his leave-taking, [the way?] on his return from here to say these
words to the Empress, in Your Majesty's letter of the 28th of last month [...], to which it came so far that Your
Majesty learned that [...] and not from him, although such words were [...] essential, which gave [him], laden with
Your Majesty's favours, [occasion?]

c042_1789-05-10.summary: Potemkin has left for the army; talks with Nassau-Siegen on the rumoured Ukrainian rising, Branicki and the withdrawal of the Russian commissariats; Stackelberg's report that the King of Prussia offers Poland help; a charge that the King wanted Branicki poisoned; 'now is the time for Poland to rise'.
c042_1789-05-10.en:
k. 138r. Yesterday morning, then, Prince Potemkin set out on his journey. May he [succeed] in it and in all his
[designs] as it shall please God; may He not mete out to him the [lot] he has deserved. But it is true that I awaited
his departure with impatience, and until it happened I held back from [reporting] to Your Majesty many things [...]
concerning him from beginning to end, and in what state they were left, which I watched; and I did not want to
describe them [...], lest he change them, for until the devil carried him off there could be no certainty about him.
I come to that description, answering first Your Majesty's letter of the 6th [...], received through the Prince of
Nassau, the other by post. What Your Majesty instructed the Prince of Nassau to tell the Empress [...] which monarchs
often use among themselves [...] proper from Your Majesty towards the Empress;

c104_1789-12-14.summary: Potemkin's courier complained of rudeness and want of horses crossing Poland; escorts for Russian couriers; Stackelberg's reports against Deboli; Deboli asks to be recalled, that the letter be burnt and the answer sent apart for him to decipher himself.
c104_1789-12-14.en:
k. 296r. At [...] a sure opportunity [...] I describe for Your Majesty's information [the matter] in which [...] I
mentioned in my letter of the 30th [...] Prince Potemkin [...] Your Majesty and Poland. When Prince Potemkin here, on
the news of the taking of Akkerman, was sending [Brigadier?] Graff [...], he instructed him expressly that he should
say before the Empress that, passing through our country, horses were given him only with great difficulty, and that
he [met with] much rudeness and insolence; and [...] he sang all this out before the monarch [...] by order of
Potemkin. And when some, surprised at it and recalling that even the ambassador [...] that escorts were ordered to be
given in our country to the Russian couriers for their safer passage, sounded him out [...] whether it was so as he
had said before the Empress,

k. 296v.
